Phugpa (ཕུག་པ, phug pa) version, computed with the arithmetic of Svante Janson, “Tibetan Calendar Mathematics” (2007, revised 2014 and 2022), epoch 806, with the moon\'s daily anomaly of 1/28 used by the Men-Tsee-Khang (སྨན་རྩིས་ཁང, sman rtsis khang) almanac. Lunar mansion, yoga, karaṇa and the lunar-day cycles follow Janson §10 and Appendix E. Checked against Janson\'s table of Losar (ལོ་གསར, lo gsar) dates for 1927–2046 and, day by day, against Edward Henning\'s computed Phugpa calendars (kalacakra.org).

Tenpō rules in Japan Standard Time: months begin on the day of new moon and are numbered by the major solar term they contain. For 2033 the leap month is 閏11月, the recommended resolution of the 2033 problem. Solar terms, new moons and 雑節 are checked against the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan (暦要項).

The almanac annotations (十二直, 二十八宿, 九星, 選日 and 暦注下段) follow the rules tabulated in Japanese Wikipedia after 岡田芳朗・阿久根末忠『現代こよみ読み解き事典』 (1993), and are checked day by day against こよみのページ (koyomi8.com). 神吉日 and 凶会日 are left out: their full rules are not recoverable.

Jean Meeus, “Astronomical Algorithms” (2nd ed., 1998): new moons from chapter 49, the sun from the VSOP87D series of Bretagnon and Francou, ΔT from the polynomials of Espenak and Meeus (NASA). Everything is computed on this phone; the app has no internet access.

The readings come from these sources; the project\'s documentation, below, names the source of each one. Japanese: こよみ博物館 of the almanac publisher Todan (六曜, 十二直, 二十八宿); Japanese Wikipedia (選日, 暦注下段, 九星, 九星気学, 歳徳神, 庚申待), whose adapted text is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; NAOJ 暦Wiki (雑節, 節句, 十三夜, 二十四節気) and koyomi8 (二十四節気); the glosses of the twenty-four terms in the Almanac Handbook (こよみ便覧, Koyomi binran) of 1787, in the public domain; the dictionaries on Kotobank. Tibetan: the translation of the hair-cutting days by Lama Zopa Rinpoche (བླ་མ་བཟོད་པ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ, bla ma bzod pa rin po che), FPMT, 2008; Edition Rabten\'s Tibetan calendar; Edward Henning\'s symbolic details of the calendar and his electional astrology of the five components (the lunar mansions and the activity lists); and the Prayer Invoking the Benefits of the Festival of the Tenth Day (ཚེས་བཅུའི་ཕན་ཡོན་གསོལ་འདེབས, tshes bcu\'i phan yon gsol \'debs) by Jigme Lingpa (འཇིགས་མེད་གླིང་པ, \'jigs med gling pa) from Lotsawa House; the colours and arrangement of the nine numbers from Alexander Berzin\'s Details of Tibetan Astrology (Study Buddhism); the four aspects and the pebbles of the day, month and year from the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) of Desi Sangye Gyatso (སྡེ་སྲིད་སངས་རྒྱས་རྒྱ་མཚོ, sde srid sangs rgyas rgya mtsho) with the Moonbeams (ཟླ་བའི་འོད་ཟེར, zla ba\'i \'od zer) of Lochen Dharmashri (ལོ་ཆེན་དྷརྨ་ཤྲཱི, lo chen d+har+ma shrI); the three humours and the six seasons of the Health screen from the Four Tantras (རྒྱུད་བཞི, rgyud bzhi) of medicine. Readings not adapted from Wikipedia are the app\'s own English summaries of the cited sources, under the app\'s licence.

The day pages and the reading sheets give the readings, not their sources. Each reading\'s source, with its pages, and the passages it rests on are in the project\'s repository: the source of every reading in the catalog (core/src/main/kotlin/zanshin/core/texts/Texts.kt), the Tibetan texts as read in docs/sources/, and the rules in docs/SPEC.md.

Tibetan terms are written in Tibetan script from their Wylie spelling, checked against the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) of Desi Sangye Gyatso (སྡེ་སྲིད་སངས་རྒྱས་རྒྱ་མཚོ, sde srid sangs rgyas rgya mtsho); their pronunciation follows the THL Simplified Phonetic Transcription of Standard Tibetan (David Germano and Nicolas Tournadre, 2003).

The tone is the day\'s for its works; it does not weigh the merit of the festival or observance.

Weighed by one rule for the day and for each work. Where the named combination of weekday and mansion and the element pair agree, the combination is the day\'s result, and what any other factor says against it is outweighed, even where the weekday and the mansion agree; it decides a work only where the element pair names it, so a lucky day keeps the date\'s and the weekday\'s prohibitions. Where the two disagree, and for every other work, the strongest factor that takes a side decides, in this order: Rāhu, the weekday, the mansion, the special days of weekday and mansion (one voice, and none when they disagree), the date, the karaṇa, the yoga and the day animal. Mixed factors are weighed by their strength, not by their number. Rāhu, the mansion and the day animal have no tone of their own and decide only the works they name; the trigram decides only works no other factor names. Outweighed factors are not shown.

One voice in the weighing: the named combination of weekday and mansion and its element pair. Where the two agree, the combination is the day\'s result, outweighing every other factor, even a good weekday and mansion; where they disagree it has no tone, and the strongest factor that takes a side decides the day.

The days are ordered by strength. First those on which the combination of weekday and mansion makes the work good: it is the result even where the planet and the mansion are each good. Then by the strongest factor naming the work good, in this order: Rāhu, the weekday, the mansion, the special days, the lunar date, the karaṇa, the yoga, the day animal, the trigram; within one rank a day whose combination is lucky comes first. Past that the order is the app\'s own: the sum of the weights of the factors on the work\'s side, ten for the combination down to one for the trigram, then the earlier day. Each day is weighed as its own page weighs it; a day no factor names is blank, not neutral.

The combination period follows the month and the hour only, so every day of a Tibetan month has the same hours; the reading of the sign then rising names the work good or to avoid, and where the work has rising signs of its own, they come first, as its particular case. The hours say when within a day, never which day: a day to avoid is not offered for its good hours.
A ring marks your enemy weekday or your death mansion: on them every work is avoided, so they are not offered. Your other days are marked and not weighed.

Named both good and to avoid

The almanac gives no order. No published rule ranks one kind of annotation above another, the lower band over the middle band or the lunar lodge over the twelve stations, so no day is called best: first come the days some annotation names good for the work and none names to avoid, then, apart, those named both ways, each in date order with both sides shown. An annotation that names everything, good or to avoid, names the work too. Only the lower band\'s own rules set some annotations aside, as on the day\'s page. A day no annotation names is blank, not neutral.
